wine.name: Goumenissa
wine.grapes: Xinomavro with Negoska, the appellation's two grapes; the law asks that Negoska make at least one part in five.
wine.sites: Family vineyards on the gentle slopes south of the town of Goumenissa, on the eastern foothills of Mount Paiko at about 200 to 250 metres, with grapes bought from growers of the zone.
wine.making: After fermentation the wine is aged for about twelve months in oak barrels, French by one merchant's sheet, before bottling. The house's Single Vineyard wine of the same two grapes is given twelve months in new French oak and six more in bottle.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry, prune and sweet tomato over violet and a touch of vanilla, with olive and mushroom as it opens; medium bodied and rounder than a Naoussa, Negoska's flesh softening Xinomavro's acidity and grip.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of the vintage thanks to its Negoska, it keeps for several years more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour or so; a Burgundy or Nebbiolo style glass.

records.table: Aidarinis is a family winery in the town of Goumenissa, and its Goumenissa is the appellation's blend of Xinomavro with Negoska, aged about a year in oak. Expect cherry, prune and sweet tomato with softer edges than a Naoussa; pour it with grilled meat.
records.story: The Aidarinis family has made wine and tsipouro, the Greek grape spirit, in Goumenissa since the late nineteenth century, by two merchants' accounts of the house. The town lies in the Kilkis regional unit on the south eastern foothills of Mount Paiko, and its partner grape, Negoska, grows almost nowhere but these slopes; its name comes from the Slavic name for Naoussa, Negush. Two merchants date the family's modern turn to 1978: the winery in its present form by one, its first vineyard planted in rows by the other. A year later, in 1979, the zone became an appellation, its rule asking that Xinomavro be joined by at least a fifth of Negoska, which brings colour and alcohol and makes the wine softer than Naoussa's. The family farms its own vineyards on the gentle slopes south of the town, at about 200 to 250 metres, and buys from growers of the zone. Its two reds of the appellation tell the district's story: the Goumenissa, a year in oak, and the Single Vineyard from one family parcel planted in 1978, given new French oak. For a sommelier, Aidarinis is the old family name of the town itself, and its Goumenissa the blend in its everyday form.

wine.name: Goumenissa
wine.grapes: Xinomavro, about seven parts in ten, with Negoska for the rest.
wine.sites: The estate's organically farmed vineyards on the Paiko foothills around Filyria, the first of them planted in 1994 at Bindabla.
wine.making: By the house's sheets the grapes are given about two days of cold soak, then the temperature is raised and fermentation runs through a long maceration on the skins. records.table: Chatzivaritis Estate farms organically at Filyria, and its Goumenissa is Xinomavro with about three parts in ten of Negoska, aged in French oak. It is fuller and riper than most Xinomavro, cherry and tomato over velvet; decant it for an hour.
records.story: The estate began as one man's hobby. Its founder, an engineer who made wine for his own pleasure, married a woman of Goumenissa and came to know its vineyards, and in 1994 he planted the first vineyard of his own at Bindabla on the Paiko foothills, farming it organically from the start. Goumenissa had by then been an appellation for fifteen years, since 1979, its red Xinomavro joined by at least a fifth of Negoska, a grape found almost nowhere but on these slopes. The family built its winery at Filyria, among the vines, and the next generation of the family has since taken the estate on. The house works the zone's grapes both together and apart. Its Goumenissa, the appellation's blend, is given a long maceration, months on its lees and French oak; around it the house bottles Negoska alone, Xinomavro alone, a Mosaic red of native and French grapes and whites with Roditis under the regional name of the Slopes of Paiko. That range has made it a teaching estate for the district: a guest can taste the two grapes of Goumenissa apart and then together. For a sommelier the Goumenissa shows the blend in a riper, fuller key, Negoska's flesh and colour set around Xinomavro's acidity.

wine.name: Goumenissa
wine.grapes: Xinomavro and Negoska, in shares that move with the vintage, from equal parts to about seven of Xinomavro to three.
wine.sites: The family's own organically farmed vineyards around Goumenissa on the foothills of Mount Paiko, worked by the family since it settled there in 1924.
wine.making: Fermented spontaneously on its own yeasts in old oak casks, unfined and unfiltered, with little or no added sulphur by the house's sheet for the 2009. The wine is then aged in used oak, about a year in one vintage, and held in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Plum compote, prune and blackberry over wet earth, worn leather, pepper and dried wildflowers; medium bodied, with high, fresh acidity and persistent, savoury tannin.
wine.ageing: Tight and savoury when young, it wants a few years in bottle; in a Greek magazine's vertical the 2003 showed fine grained tannin and concentration, while the 2000 had passed its peak.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle to let it breathe and an older one off its sediment; a Burgundy or Nebbiolo style glass.

records.table: Tatsis is a family estate of Goumenissa farmed organically, and its Goumenissa is Xinomavro and Negoska fermented on wild yeasts in old oak and bottled unfiltered. It is earthy and savoury, plum and leather over fresh acidity; decant it and give it time.
records.story: The family came to Goumenissa as refugees. By the family's account, in the population exchanges of 1924 the grandparents left Ano Vodeno in Eastern Rumelia and settled in the town, whose vineyards, as the house tells it, reminded them of home, and they grew vines there for the next two generations. Goumenissa became an appellation in 1979, its red Xinomavro joined by at least a fifth of Negoska. In 1996 two grandsons took over the family estate from their father and made their first vintage, and their Goumenissa followed in the late 1990s. In 1998 the vineyards were certified organic, and in 2002 the family turned to biodynamic farming. In the cellar the brothers chose to leave the wine alone: wild yeasts, old oak casks, no fining or filtering and little or no added sulphur, and long enough in bottle that the wine reaches the market with some age. That way of working put the house among the names of Greece's natural wine movement, and its wines have been poured at natural wine fairs abroad, RAW among them. For a sommelier Tatsis is Goumenissa without polish: savoury, earthy and alive, the blend for a guest who likes Xinomavro raw and true to its village.

records.story: Mikro Ktima Titos, the small estate of Titos, carries the name of the grower who founded the winery at the foot of Mount Paiko, among old oak trees beside the river Sirios, near the hamlet of Dyo Potamia. By the estate's own account, as two guides give it, he planted its first vineyard beside the river in 1972; seven years later, in 1979, the zone became an appellation, its red Xinomavro joined by at least a fifth of Negoska. After the founder's death the property passed, in 2018, to the founders of Ktima Biblia Chora, the estate on the slopes of Mount Pangeon in eastern Macedonia, who revived the winery under the name Mikro Ktima Titos. The new owners kept it small and to two reds. The Goumenissa holds to the appellation's classic share of about one part Negoska to four of Xinomavro and is aged mostly in large French casks, so that fruit leads and wood stays behind; beside it stands a Negoska bottled on its own, a rare chance to taste the district's second grape apart. The estate receives visitors for tours and tastings, and its Goumenissa has travelled to merchants in Britain. For a sommelier, Titos is Goumenissa in its supple, modern form: fruit first, silky tannin, a red that pours well by the glass.

records.story: Boutari is the Naoussa house founded in 1879, and Naoussa's Xinomavro made its name. Goumenissa, to the north east on the foothills of Mount Paiko in Kilkis, became an appellation in 1979, its red Xinomavro joined by at least a fifth of Negoska. In 1984 the house's own winery in the district began to work, and by the house's own account, which Wines of Greece repeats, it was for many years the only winery in the area. In 1991 the house planted Domaine Filyria, its own vineyard beside the village of that name, mostly with Xinomavro and Negoska and with trial rows of Chardonnay, Syrah, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, and farmed it organically; the house calls it a model vineyard for the region. The house had bottled a plain Goumenissa, met in America in vintages of the 1990s, and Filiria became the estate's own wine: the two grapes from the organic vines, aged a year and more in French oak. In the 1990s smaller family estates began to bottle their own Goumenissa beside it, Chatzivaritis and Tatsis among them. For a sommelier, Filiria is the large house's Goumenissa, and a reminder that Boutari's Xinomavro reaches beyond Naoussa into the blend of its northern neighbour.

report: Pick in doubt, as the plan says: Boutari is Naoussa's pick too, with the Grande Reserve as its flagship there, so this record takes the Goumenissa estate wine Filiria and never the Naoussa wines; a Greek account gives the district five wineries in all, which are this group's five, so no sixth house stands ready if the merge agent drops it.

The wine is Filiria rather than the plain Boutari Goumenissa: the house's Goumenissa page and Wines of Greece both name the estate Domaine Filyria, and the plain Goumenissa was met only in American listings of the 1990s and 2001.

Neither wine could be confirmed as still made: the house's own wine pages found carry no Goumenissa, and the one Filiria listing read was the 2008, sold out; the refuter should confirm the wine is still bottled before it ships.
That Filiria carries the Goumenissa PDO rests on one merchant and its blend; the label's exact wording was not seen.

A share of equal parts and the 5.5 hectare vineyard rest on single listings and are left out; the land bought at the end of the 1980s and an investment in the mid 1970s rest on one account each and are left out.
Founded is 1984, the winery's start by the house and Wines of Greece, not 1879, the Naoussa house's founding; the founder of 1879 is not named because his dates were not sourced here.

changed: story: Aidarinis was said to have grown up around the Boutari winery since 1984; merchants date the Aidarinis winery to 1978 and the family to the late nineteenth century, so the line now names the estates that began bottling in the 1990s, Chatzivaritis (first vineyard 1994) and Tatsis (first vintage 1996).
story: the only winery claim is now said to be the house's, repeated by Wines of Greece, as both search summaries read.
open: Filiria is still made: not confirmed. The house's page names the estate and its organic vineyard, a Cypriot importer lists Filiria in its portfolio, but no vintage after 2008 was found; the integrator should confirm before it ships.
The pick stays in doubt for the merge agent, as the author says: Boutari is Naoussa's pick too.
